# The van almost caught fire while I was drying a dog

Last Wednesday, October 28, at about 2:15 in the afternoon, I was in a client’s driveway in Bedford drying Moose, a very good Bernese Mountain Dog, on high.

Then I smelled hot plastic.

At first I thought it was the dryer motor. I’ve used that dryer so many times that my brain reached for the most familiar explanation. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where my batteries are.

I turned off the battery switch and got Moose out through the side door. He was still damp and, honestly, thrilled to be outside. I used the fire extinguisher. I was shaking so hard I could barely think. Moose’s mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I tried to calm down.

Everyone is okay. That’s what matters most. But the inverter cable had overheated. Its insulation had melted back about three centimetres, and the positive lug was black. The van is off the road while I wait for repairs, and I’ve already cancelled 31 appointments. My whole income comes from this van. Rent is due on the first. I’m scared, angry, and still trying to work out what comes next.

I’m writing this because I don’t want another groomer to have to learn about their van’s electrical system this way.

I’m not an electrician. I’m a mobile dog groomer who trusted a tidy-looking build. This is what I understand so far from the electrician who inspected it, and what she told me to ask about. Please treat this as one person’s account—not a diagnosis of your van, or instructions to repair one yourself.

## What was in my van

My van had a 3,000-watt inverter and two 200 amp-hour lithium batteries in a 12-volt system. It was built by Coastline Van Fitouts in spring 2025. The cable running from the battery bank to the inverter was 4 AWG. The fuse was a 300-amp ANL fuse, mounted about 90 centimetres from the battery.

My dryer draws around 1,800–2,000 watts. I also sometimes use the water heater. I didn’t understand, before this happened, how much current that kind of equipment asks a 12-volt system to carry.

Here’s the basic relationship:

**Watts ÷ volts = amps.**

At 12 volts, a 1,800-watt load works out to 150 amps, and a 2,000-watt load works out to about 167 amps—before accounting for the fact that an inverter isn’t perfectly efficient and that the battery voltage can change under load. In real use, the current drawn from the batteries can be higher. Add another high-wattage appliance and the total can climb further.

That doesn’t mean anyone can look at those numbers and safely choose a cable or fuse. The right cable size depends on more than the inverter’s headline wattage: things like the actual load, cable length, installation conditions, allowable voltage drop, and the equipment manufacturer’s requirements all matter. A qualified person needs to assess the whole system.

Priya, the electrician who inspected my van, told me that the 4 AWG cable in my installation was too small for this 3,000-watt, 12-volt inverter setup, and that she would expect 2/0 cable for it. That is what she told me about *my installation*; it isn’t a universal rule for every van. Ask a qualified installer to calculate and specify the right cable for your actual system, and get that specification in writing.

The lug at the positive end of my cable was another concern. Priya said it appeared to have been crimped with something like pliers or a hammer rather than a proper crimping tool. Heat-shrink tubing covered the connection, so it looked finished from the outside. Heat-shrink can protect and tidy a connection, but it can’t make a poor crimp sound.

The fuse location was also flagged. Mine was about 90 centimetres from the battery. Priya said it should have been much closer—around 18 centimetres in my setup. Exact requirements depend on the applicable standard, the installation and the equipment. Don’t take my measurement and use it as a universal specification. Ask your installer where the overcurrent protection needs to go and why.

The repair quote is $4,200. It includes rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block and a Class T fuse. Parts are on order, and I’ve been told to expect at least three weeks. I’m waiting to hear more from insurance; the adjuster is coming Thursday.

## What we know—and what we don’t

The sequence I experienced was: I was running the dryer, smelled hot plastic, then saw smoke from the battery bench. After the incident, the positive lug was black and the cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres. Priya inspected the system and identified the cable size, the lug and the fuse location as concerns.

I can tell you those facts. I can’t tell you, on my own, precisely how the failure started or assign a definitive cause. I’m not qualified to do that, and I don’t want to pretend otherwise. A professional needs to assess the equipment and damage.

I also want to be fair about the builder. Darren at Coastline Van Fitouts hasn’t answered three texts and an email so far. That’s where things stand as I write this. I’m not trying to trash him publicly or tell anyone what to think. I’m sharing what was in my van, what happened, what the electrician told me, and what I’m doing next. People can make their own decisions with those facts.

I trusted the build because it looked tidy. The wiring was hidden away, and the finished van looked professional. But tidy is not the same as right. A clean-looking installation doesn’t tell you whether the cable is correctly sized, whether a connection was made with the right tool, or whether the fuse is properly located and rated.

Priya showed me photos of the damage beside thermal-camera images from her own van while it was running a similar kind of load. Her cable barely warmed up. The contrast was wild. That comparison helped me see why the details matter, but it’s not a test you can use to certify your own system. A cable that feels cool—or appears cool in one photo—doesn’t prove the whole installation is safe.

I bought a basic infrared thermometer at Canadian Tire for about $40. It can be useful for noticing a hot surface, but it cannot tell you whether your wiring is correctly designed or safely installed. Please don’t use one to test a cable under load, open a live electrical compartment, or decide that a system is fine because one reading looks normal. If something smells hot, looks damaged, smokes, or seems wrong, stop using the system and get qualified help.

## What you can check without taking anything apart

This is not a DIY electrical inspection. It’s a list of questions and observations you can make without opening covers, removing fuses or touching wiring. If you’re unsure whether something is safe to approach, leave it alone and call a qualified professional.

**With the system switched off and no appliances running:**

- Look for visible damage from a safe distance: melted or discoloured insulation, blackened areas, scorching, a burnt-plastic smell, or smoke residue. Don’t touch damaged wiring.
- Notice whether battery or electrical covers are missing, loose or damaged. Don’t remove a cover to look inside.
- Check whether your van has a working smoke alarm that can be heard from the grooming area. Mine only had the one in the cab that came with the van. I should have asked whether that was enough coverage for the way I use the vehicle.
- Find out where your battery shutoff is and make sure you know how to use it. Ask your installer to walk you through what it does—and what it does not disconnect.
- Ask a qualified installer to document the inverter model and rating, battery configuration, cable sizes and lengths, fuse types and ratings, and fuse locations.
- Ask what loads your system was designed to run at the same time. A dryer and water heater can be a very different demand from one appliance alone.
- Ask what to do if you smell hot plastic, see smoke, or hear an alarm. Keep the plan simple and make sure anyone who works with you knows it.
- Keep the appropriate fire extinguisher accessible and learn how it’s meant to be used. If there’s smoke or a fire, prioritize getting yourself, your clients and the dogs away from danger and calling emergency services. Don’t put yourself at risk trying to save equipment.

Don’t remove a fuse to check its rating, pull on a cable, retighten a connection, or try to inspect a lug beneath heat-shrink. Even with the system switched off, batteries can still supply dangerous current, and a “power off” switch may not isolate every part of the installation. A qualified person can tell you how your specific system should be made safe before inspection.

## Tasha, please ask before you pay a deposit

Tasha is about to put a deposit down with the same builder who did my van. I’m not telling her what to decide. I am asking her—and any groomer planning a build—to get the electrical details in writing *before* paying.

Ask the builder:

- What exact inverter and battery system are you proposing?
- What cable size and length will connect the batteries to the inverter, and how was that selected for my loads?
- What fuse or breaker will protect that cable, what is its rating and type, and where will it be installed?
- What loads is the system designed to run at the same time?
- Who is doing the electrical work, and what qualifications or credentials do they have?
- Will I get a wiring diagram, equipment list and written specifications when the build is finished?
- Who do I contact if I notice a hot smell, an alarm or a problem after delivery?

You don’t have to know the technical answer yourself. The point is to ask for one, in plain language, from the person designing and installing the system—and to have it documented. If an answer is unclear, ask them to explain it. If you want a second opinion, arrange one with a qualified electrician or marine electrician before the build is signed off.

## Where I’m at

I’m still shaken. I keep replaying how quickly the smell turned into smoke, and I’m grateful Moose’s mom was there with me. Moose got out safely, though he went home damp. His opinion of the whole adventure was apparently excellent.

For now, the van is parked. I’ve cancelled 31 appointments, I’m waiting on the adjuster, and I’m trying to manage the repair costs and the lost work. The current quote is $4,200 to rewire the main runs, replace the fuse block and install a Class T fuse. Parts are on order, and the minimum timeline I’ve been given is three weeks. I’ll share more when I know what insurance is covering and when the van will be ready.

I’ll also post an update when I have the repair details and can get back on the road. Until then, please ask questions about your own build while you still have time to ask them. Don’t rely on how tidy the wiring looks. Get the specifications in writing, and have a qualified professional look at your system.

I’m a groomer, not an electrician. I’m sharing what happened to me so other groomers can have a better conversation with their builders—not so anyone tries to repair a high-current system themselves.
